The FIA’s automated blue flag system encountered an issue during last Sunday’s race at the Hungaroring, forcing lapped cars to be notified manually by the marshalling posts. This led to a number of issues with lapped cars getting in the way, with the most notable example being the clash between Carlos Sainz and Oscar Piastri. Show X Embedded Content Loading this video will expose you to potential cookies and tracking by the provider Sainz said it was “impossible to avoid” the incident, though onboard footage later showed that the Williams driver was given plenty of blue flags and was warned by his engineer that Piastri was behind. Piastri fumed at Sainz, stating: "Yeah, I knew there were blue flag [issues], but there were blue flags on all the marshal signals. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT "I was right behind him. I couldn't believe what happened. Getting crashed into by a lapped car is never one of the things you expect that can go wrong in your race. “I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no one told him or there was a lack of complete awareness is unacceptable." Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff criticised engineers as “Teletubbies” for not doing enough to warn their drivers they were about to be lapped. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “It was like first day of school! And I'm talking kindergarten in the way that drivers were reacting to blue flags. “Now, some will say the timing streams had an issue. One of the eight blue flag signals missed by Sainz © F1 “But there is such a thing as just being spatially aware, and your engineers actually looking over the pit wall, and I made this comment in commentary: very few of the teams now actually have a gap on their, what is affectionately known as, prat perch, the engineering wall where the engineers and the team principal normally sit. “In the case of Toto [Wolff], of course, he's sitting back in the garage, but they look, and they did look over the pit wall back in the day, and you have a certain awareness of where the other cars are. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “So, you can't ever factor in qualifying on somebody coming out of the pit lane. “But in a grand prix, when people are circulating at pace, you can usually tell. Well, not usually – you absolutely can tell! https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The Minnesota state capitol in St Paul, Minnesota. Photograph: EJ_Rodriquez/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Minnesota state capitol in St Paul, Minnesota. Photograph: EJ_Rodriquez/Getty Images US midterm elections 2026 Minnesota primaries could mark change of path for Democrats and Republicans From progressive and moderate to election deniers, state sees wide spectrum of candidates in test of direction for both parties Rachel Leingang Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Minnesota voters on both sides of the aisle are weighing the direction of their parties – and their chances of winning over the general electorate – in marquee statewide races on Tuesday. On the left, Peggy Flanagan, the state lieutenant governor and a progressive, faces off against Angie Craig, a US representative, for the Democratic bid for US senate in a race punctuated by the role of immigration enforcement in the state that saw two residents killed by immigration agents in a winter surge. On the right, Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, carries Donald Trump’s endorsement in a three-way race for the Republican nomination for governor, where Republicans face an uphill battle to challenge Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic contender and a US senator, now seeking the governor’s office. Will democratic socialist Francesca Hong shake up the establishment – or help Republicans win Wisconsin? Read more After Tuesday, the general election for the open governor and US senate seats will shape up, signaling a change for top roles in the state. Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat, initially sought a third term, but dropped his bid after ongoing fraud scandals threatened to distract from the race. Tina Smith, the Democratic US senator, decided not to run again , saying she wanted to spend time with her grandkids and make way for new faces in the chamber. She has endorsed Flanagan. The state leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor. A Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972. Still, Republicans hope to seize on fraud problems in state programs, including criminal cases against a sprawling group accused of organized theft of meals for children, services for kids with autism and housing programs. US Senate race While Republicans have a primary for US senate on Tuesday as well, Michele Tafoya, a former National Football League sideline reporter, is likely to be the GOP nominee. On the Democratic side, polls of the race have been mixed . Flanagan has attacked Craig for supporting the Laken Riley Act, a federal law that requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, named after a woman murdered in Georgia by an undocumented immigrant. Craig has since expressed regret for her vote, writing in March that it has “become clear that supporting any bill that gives ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] new authority in this administration was the wrong decision”. Flanagan told the Guardian she appreciated that Craig has said she regrets the vote, but that she thinks Craig owes Minnesotans an apology and that the vote showed “a real lack of judgment”. “I also think it shows a pretty big disconnect from Minnesotans and the communities here,” Flanagan said. “I think it demonstrates that she doesn’t have a lot of relationships with the people who are most impacted. I think that matters.” Craig has gone after Flanagan on the fraud issue, saying Flanagan has not taken accountability for any role that allowed fraud to perpetuate. “State fraud is the No 1 issue as Minnesota voters go to the polls in November,” Craig told the New York Times . “Fairly or not, the lieutenant governor has a unique vulnerability as our statewide Senate candidate because she’s been helping run the state for the last eight years.” Craig was not available for an interview with the Guardian. The 54-year-old was first elected to congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to US Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide. Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation and began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins. “My job, as soon as I get to Washington DC, is to have 99 cups of coffee with people, to build those relationships, to find opportunities for common ground with folks on the other side of the aisle,” she said. “We may find some unexpected places to work together.” Her platform now includes support for the proposed Medicare for All system of universal healthcare, an issue that she didn’t start off her campaign supporting, but embraced after talking to people across the state who had healthcare horror stories. “They want folks who aren’t going to govern by sternly worded letter,” Flanagan said. “And I think that people are ready for big, bold change.” Tafoya, a Republican who is pro-choice, is counting on winning over independent voters. She has centered her campaign on the fraud scandals. Republican delegates at the state convention endorsed Adam Schwarze, a Marine and Navy Seal. Governor’s race Lindell, the pillow salesman, is hoping to ride Trump’s endorsement to a victory over Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, and Kendall Qualls, a businessman. Qualls won the endorsement of Republican activists at the state party convention earlier this year. Lindell has faced opposition from the state Republican party, which has questioned his eligibility to hold office in the state, saying it wanted clarity on whether Lindell has lived in Minnesota long enough to qualify. Lindell, who is from Minnesota, has also lived in Texas. He has said he moved back to Minnesota in August 2025, though only registered to vote in the state in July 2026. Lindell, who has been sued for defamation by voting machine companies and others , has not relented in his claims that the 2020 election was stolen and that Trump had actually won. He currently faces allegations of a potential campaign finance law violation over handing out free pillows at a parade. An administrative law judge in the state recently said there was “probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election”. Lindell called the complaint “complete nonsense”. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, saying he needed to focus on his campaign for governor. He also faces millions in creditor claims over unpaid bills from the company. Alex Plechash, the Minnesota Republican party chair, said Trump’s endorsement of Lindell was a “surprise” and noted that Lindell has “significant electability concerns”. Klobuchar faces several Democratic contenders in a primary, though is likely to easily win on Tuesday. Klobuchar, who ran for president in 2020, has handily won her US Senate campaigns since she was first elected in 2006. Congressional races Multiple congressional districts in Minnesota have contested Democratic primaries on Tuesday as well. In Craig’s congressional district, the second district south of Minneapolis-St. Paul, three people with experience in the statehouse are running. Matt Little, a former state senator, Kaela Berg, a state representative, and Matt Klein, a state senator, are vying for the seat. Both Little and Berg spent time during Operation Metro Surge patrolling ICE activity. Outside spending has flooded the race in recent days. While the district is seen as purple, Cook Political Report rated it as a likely Democratic seat this cycle. In southern Minnesota’s first congressional district, previously represented by Walz, Jake Johnson, a high school math teacher, is hoping he can flip a seat now held by Brad Finstad, a Republican, though he first needs to beat Alex Eaton in the Democratic primary. In the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota’s Iron Range, Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, faces Luke Gulbranson, who has been on reality TV show Summer House. The winner will face Pete Stauber, the Republican representative for the area, in a solidly red district. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crk5.text: Image source, ABC News/Jamie McKinnell Image caption, Ahmed al Ahmed, outside a local Sydney court, welcomed the decision on Wednesday By Lana Lam Sydney Published 4 hours ago A man who was hailed a hero for disarming one of the Bondi Beach shooters in December has had assault charges against him dropped by police. Ahmed al Ahmed was charged in June with domestic violence common assault, as well as stalking and intimidation, after an alleged incident with his father in March at a home in southwest Sydney. Ahmed denied both charges. On Wednesday, in a local Sydney court, prosecutors withdrew the charges after it was agreed that Ahmed would abide by an apprehended domestic violence order for 12 months, limiting his contact with his father. Outside the court, Ahmed, 44, welcomed the development, telling reporters that he was a "free man" and that he hoped for "peace". Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr said in court that the order prohibiting Ahmed from assaulting, threatening, stalking or intimidating his father had been accepted without admissions, according to national broadcaster ABC. Ahmed made global headlines last year after footage emerged of him tackling one of two gunmen who had opened fire during a Jewish event at Sydney's Bondi Beach, killing 15 people. Figure caption, Watch: Eyewitness captures moment man tackles and disarms Bondi shooter Ahmed wrestled a firearm from Sajid Akram and was later shot several times by a second alleged gunman, Naveed Akram. The attack marked Australia's deadliest mass shooting in decades, and police later declared it a terrorist incident targeting the Jewish community. A fundraiser in the days after the shooting raised more than AU$2.5m ($1.7m; Â£1.24m) for Ahmed, who also received a bedside visit from Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. In a separate court matter, two of Ahmed's brothers were recently charged over allegations they threatened him and tried to extort some of the donations he had received. https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141066.text: Russian missiles reportedly enter Nato airspace amid massive strike as Volodymyr Zelensky rallies allies for help ‘It is important that our partners fully understand what is happening and that the protection of lives directly depends on their readiness, said Zelensky’ On Thursday, Russia reportedly launched a heavy bombardment across Ukraine, prompting NATO allies' jets to scramble fighter jets as a precautionary measure to protect the bloc’s airspace amid the massive attack. The President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky released an emergency plea to his allies for help as he revealed his air force had alerted him to a higher probability of Vladimir Putin during the early hours of the morning today. In this connection, he posted on social media: “It is important that our partners fully understand what is happening and that the protection of lives directly depends on their readiness or lack thereof to help us with air defense missiles.” Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also confirmed the Ukrainian capital had come under major attack from Russian ballistic missiles. The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces released a statement that it had deployed assets and resources at its disposal to address the threat. Zelensky’s appeals to allies follow his visit to the White House on Tuesday. He sat down with Trump in the Oval Office to discuss per mission pacts for the production of Patriot interceptors. Notably, only Patriot systems are neutralizing Russian missiles, but Ukraine fell short of PAC-3 interceptor missiles. According to the Ukrainian President, he had a “good meeting” with his American counterpart. He is now counting on practical results after Tuesday’s meeting in Washington. It is pertinent to mention here that relations between Mr. Zelensky and the US President have improved since the infamous outburst in the Oval Office at the beginning of his second term. Additionally, Trump had previously committed to grant Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot air defense systems domestically. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98v.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Firefighters battle a blaze at warehouse in Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday By Harry Sekulich Published 20 August 2026, 02:43 BST Updated 1 hour ago A wave of overnight Russian missile strikes has killed at least eight people in the capital Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian authorities say. Apartment blocks and warehouses were hit in the "massive attack" on Thursday, according to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS), while a children's hospital and school were damaged. At least 33 people were injured. Authorities are working to rescue people trapped underneath the rubble of demolished buildings, with crews already pulling two survivors from debris. Meanwhile, Romania said one drone crossed into its territory at the northern border with Ukraine triggering an air alert siren. In the early hours of Thursday, "a drone entered Romanian national airspace, approximately 13 kilometres east of the city of GalaÈi," the Romanian defence ministry wrote in a statement. The drone crashed into "an uninhabited area", causing a small fire that was extinguished. "No casualties or material damage were reported", the ministry added, noting that the initial alert had been lifted. The Polish military also said it had begun "defensive air operations" to protect its airspace, with the country sharing part of its south-eastern border with Ukraine. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Kyiv resident took shelter underground as sirens blared across the capital Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said a children's hospital had been damaged in the overnight strikes, where windows were broken and cars set ablaze nearby. There was also damage at an educational institution, he said. An industrial centre in the Solomyanskyi district, south-west Kyiv, was also hit by missiles, according to the mayor. An attack in Brovary district of the broader Kyiv region killed one man and wounded another, Kyiv regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. The regional administration issued an alert earlier in the night warning residents to take shelter. It continued: "Air defense operations are possible in the area". More missile alerts were issued from regional authorities throughout the night, citing warnings from the Ukrainian air force that missiles were flying towards the capital. The Russian airstrikes cut power to thousands of properties overnight, plunging parts of the Kyiv region into darkness, with technicians racing to repair the damaged energy grids. The Russian defence ministry claims to have targeted a drone component production facility and a munition depot in Kyiv, according to state-run media, although the claims have not been independently verified by the BBC. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Cars erupt in flames during overnight strikes in Kyiv Kyiv has been battered in near nightly-attacks in recent weeks, with some strikes resulting in dozens of deaths and serious injuries. More than a dozen regions have been targeted across Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, with Russia launching more than 1,550 attack drones, 1,560 guide aerial bombs and 62 missiles Ukraine. Ukraine has stepped up its attacks deep inside Russia during the past few weeks, with a recent flurry of 600 drones targeting Moscow. Two separate attacks on Russia this week has killed at least 16 people, including one child. Since July, Ukraine has repeatedly targeted a warehouse belonging to the online retailer Wildberries, known as Russia's version of Amazon. Ukraine's defence ministry said the latest attack meant that seven out of 10 of the largest Wildberries logistics centres had been "disabled". While the attacks on Russia are partly intended to increase pressure on Moscow to engage in peace talks to end the four and a half year war, there has been little movement on diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire deal. Both sides accuse each other of targeting civilians. Russia first launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory â largely concentrated in the eastern border regions. From August 16 to August 22, 2026, supporters of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI) and the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (PMOI/MEK) held coordinated demonstrations, sit-ins, and public exhibitions across major cities in Europe and North America. Amplifying the voice of an exhausted public undergoing severe socio-economic hardship and brutal state violence under the newly installed supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, these global actions demanded an immediate end to executions, called for the closure of Iranian diplomatic missions functioning as espionage hubs, and pressed the international community to recognize the Iranian people’s demand for a secular, democratic republic. August 21, 2026 In Berlin , supporters of the NCRI continued their ongoing sit-in outside the Iranian regime’s embassy, marking nearly half a year of continuous demonstration against state violence, systemic executions, and diplomatic appeasement. Demonstrators reiterated demands for the complete closure of the embassy, characterizing it as a center for espionage and state-sponsored terrorism, while advocating for a democratic republic based on NCRI President-elect Maryam Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan . In Paris , activists organized a book stand and photo exhibition highlighting the continuing detention of protesters arrested during the January 2026 uprising and the surge in death sentences under the clerical dictatorship. A similar educational initiative was launched in Winchester , United Kingdom, where the Academics in Exile Association held a photo exhibition that drew strong public engagement, collecting signatures on petitions calling for United Nations intervention against state repression. Simultaneously, broad rallies and solidarity demonstrations under the global “No to Executions” campaign were conducted across Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen, and The Hague , with NCRI Nordic representative Parviz Khazaei calling for decisive international action against Tehran’s apparatus of terror. In tandem, coordinated commemorations honoring the martyrs of the 1988 massacre and fallen dissidents took place in Berlin, Bern, Aarhus, Paris, Rome, Munich, Toronto, and Ottawa , where crowds chanted slogans rejecting both monarchical autocracy and theocratic rule. Irvine, California: Iranian-Americans Rally in Support of the “No to Execution Tuesdays” Campaign August 20, 2026 Marking its 173rd consecutive day, the embassy sit-in in Berlin maintained its persistent presence, with protesters emphasizing that Western governments must halt policies of appeasement toward Tehran and support the Iranian people’s drive for a secular democracy. In Paris , NCRI supporters convened another photo exhibition and outreach drive, presenting the platform of the Iranian Resistance as the definitive path toward justice, peace, and fundamental civil liberties while condemning ongoing human rights abuses against political prisoners inside Iran. August 19, 2026 Gathering at Dam Square in Amsterdam , Iranian expatriates and resistance supporters organized a public demonstration aligned with the “No to Executions Tuesdays” movement, demanding the immediate abolition of capital punishment and the release of all political detainees. Demonstrators emphasized that neither the return of the monarchy nor the continuation of the ruling theocracy reflects the will of the Iranian public. Meanwhile, in Paris , activists maintained public outreach through photo displays and book stands, exposing the regime’s escalating execution rates designed to quell internal discontent following the January 2026 nationwide uprising. August 18, 2026 In Gothenburg, NCRI supporters rallied in solidarity with the 134th week of the “No to Executions Tuesdays” campaign, warning of the grave, immediate danger facing political prisoners across Iran’s security dungeons and voicing explicit support for the MEK Resistance Units active inside the country. Across the Atlantic in Toronto , Canadian Member of Parliament and former minister Judy Sgro joined members of the Iranian-Canadian community at Queen’s Park for a solemn gathering and exhibition marking the 38th anniversary of the 1988 massacre of over 30,000 political prisoners, while demanding an end to the current wave of executions. In Irvine , California, Iranian-American activists hosted a rally and memorial photo display, honoring executed protesters and reaffirming their commitment to establishing a democratic, secular republic in Iran. August 16, 2026 Immediate protests erupted outside Iranian diplomatic facilities in response to the hanging earlier that day of protester Shahram Sadeghi , who had been detained during the January 2026 uprising. Outside the Iranian embassy in Oslo , demonstrators joined by NCRI Nordic representative Parviz Khazaei condemned Sadeghi’s execution, called for the immediate release of all political prisoners, and demanded the closure of the embassy as a hub of state intelligence operations. Outside Sweden’s Foreign Ministry in Stockholm , demonstrators similarly gathered with photographs of executed dissidents, urging the Swedish government to adopt a firm policy against Tehran’s state-sanctioned violence. In Berlin , where supporters marked the 164th day of their ongoing embassy sit-in, protesters held an emergency rally condemning Sadeghi’s execution and reiterating calls for an end to Western appeasement. August 15, 2026 Reports received during the current reporting cycle detailed multiple major rallies and exhibitions held earlier in August. In Paris , an exhibition at Place Joachim-du-Bellay focused on the dramatic surge in state executions since early 2026, framed within the broader destabilization following the conflict between Iran and the United States that began on February 28. In Bern , supporters gathered to honor the victims of the 1988 massacre and pay tribute to Hossein Shariati , a longtime PMOI member who recently passed away after decades of opposition activity. In Munich , a photo exhibition drew attention to the thousands of casualties reported during the crackdown on the January 2026 uprising alongside the victims of 1988. In Bucharest , Romanian citizens joined Iranian expatriates at a public exhibition urging an international tribunal to prosecute senior Iranian officials for crimes against humanity. The widespread international mobilization across European capitals and North American cities demonstrates that the Iranian democratic opposition has successfully established a synchronized global counterweight to Tehran’s authoritarian apparatus. As the clerical regime faces insurmountable domestic pressure—driven by severe economic collapse, public exhaustion, and escalating internal strikes—its attempt to project authority through capital punishment and overseas intelligence networks has only deepened its international isolation. The persistence of long-term sit-ins and coordinated diaspora actions underscores that the struggle inside Iran is inextricably linked to a global diplomatic push that rejects both theocratic tyranny and monarchical restoration. Despite the regime’s efforts to silence internal dissent through state terror, the global campaign highlights an undeniable reality: Tehran’s strategy of coercion has failed to suppress the demand for a free, secular, and democratic republic. https://focustaiwan.tw:443/politics/2026.text: INTERVIEW / Taiwan eyeing global drone role via partnerships: Vice President Hsiao Taipei, Aug. 26 (CNA) Taiwan should leverage its strengths in cybersecurity and pursue international partnerships to secure a central role in the global drone supply chain as demand for drones booms worldwide, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) has said. Foreign governments and companies have not only purchased drones but also key components, including sensing modules, propulsion systems and flight-control systems, from Taiwan in recent years, Hsiao told CNA in an interview on Aug. 21. "They've come to Taiwan mainly because they think Taiwan can provide more trustworthy non-red supply chains," Hsiao said, referring to drone supply chains that do not rely on Chinese components. The vice president characterized Taiwan's desire to build an international drone presence as an effort to capitalize on growing commercial opportunities, as unmanned vehicles become increasingly important in warfare and other facets of life. "I believe the future (of drones) lies not only in military applications, but also in the vast opportunities offered by civilian markets across various sectors," Hsiao said. "These opportunities could enable Taiwan to shape a new industry with significant business potential." ● Taiwan eyeing global drone role via partnerships: Vice President Hsiao Given the apparent urgency to develop the sector, Taiwan has been encouraging drone manufacturers to obtain U.S.-administered cybersecurity certifications. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Economic Affairs' Industrial Development Administration led 12 manufacturers to Washington, D.C., to learn about the Blue UAS certification criteria established by the U.S. Defense Innovation Unit and market demand. "Drones are not used only for military purposes...They are also used for inspections and in areas involving privacy and public safety," Hsiao said. "Buyers want the payloads, sensors and data-transmission systems on drones to have a certain level of trustworthiness." Meanwhile, technological partnerships and original equipment manufacturing (OEM) arrangements have emerged as forms of international cooperation in drone production, Hsiao said. Technological cooperation allows Taiwanese and foreign drone manufacturers to complement each other's strengths, she said, adding that such partnerships could strengthen both sides' positions in the global market. International cooperation, including the procurement of dual-use drones through direct commercial sales, can also help Taiwan quickly develop capabilities it lacks in drone warfare, Hsiao said. Though Taiwan's drone sector has its strengths, it also has gaps that still need to be filled. In April, Chiou Chyou-huey (邱求慧), director-general of the Industrial Development Administration, said the government was funding manufacturers to develop AI imaging modules and chips, flight control systems and modules, and other items to close key technological gaps. He expected Taiwan to acquire the capability to manufacture critical components it currently sources from overseas by March 2027. Drone testing Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim speaks during an interview with CNA at the Presidential Office in Taipei on Aug. 21, where she discussed Taiwan's efforts to expand domestic drone production and deepen international cooperation. CNA photo Aug. 21, 2026 Hsiao said testing is another crucial area in drone development that Taiwan could use to deepen cooperation with like-minded international partners. Taiwan has "crowded" airspace where drone testing could potentially affect aviation and residential safety, Hsiao said. Taiwan could bring its drones to like-minded countries with larger airspaces to test new technology, potentially in environments involving GPS interference or more complex electromagnetic conditions, and then bring them back for improvements, Hsiao said. "Many people tell us that Ukrainian drone technology has developed so quickly because they test their drones every day. They do not have to go through applications or obtain airspace approvals," Hsiao said. "Everything we are doing is intended to prevent us from ending up in Ukraine's situation. We do not want to have to use battlefields and bloodshed to validate the capabilities of our drones." As Hsiao sees it, Taiwan's ability to conduct R&D as well as OEM and serial production is a major reason why international companies trust it as a reliable co-production partner. Taiwan's R&D capabilities, in particular, have matured to the point where it could "gradually overtake" its competitors technically, she said. The country's drone industry must, therefore, complete its skill set if it is to compete with leaders in the industry such as China, the U.S. and Ukraine, Hsiao argued. Taiwanese military service member operates a drone. Photo courtesy of the Army Matsu Defense Command "One key area is AI," noted Hsiao, calling it a main driving force behind drone evolution, with new drone technology emerging on the battlefield of the Russia-Ukraine war every few weeks. Hsiao said Taiwan is expected to play a "key role" in the development of AI-powered drones and identified edge computing, on-device AI and embodied AI as critical emerging technologies that can be applied to drones. Though Taiwan is a relatively latecomer to drone manufacturing, Hsiao said she was confident that the country will soon catch up with the competition, noting that the drone industry has posted rapid growth. "The volume of drones we exported in the first half of this year has already exceeded the volume exported during all of last year," Hsiao said. Much of that growth, however, has been driven by warfare or demand from countries in regions facing conflict. In the first seven months of 2026, unmanned aircraft exports totaled US$241.39 million, up 1,239 percent from the US$18.03 million shipped in the same period in 2025, according to International Trade Administration statistics. Of the total, 75.6 percent by value was shipped to the Czech Republic (US$137.17 million) and Poland (US$45.31 million), and the drones were likely eventually destined for Ukraine, according to defense analysts. Another US$47.18 million worth of drones was shipped to Saudi Arabia, all in June 2026, the statistics showed. Drone diplomacy Taiwan Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim outlines Taiwan's plans to strengthen its drone industry during an interview with CNA at the Presidential Office in Taipei on Aug. 21. CNA photo Aug. 21, 2026 Asked about Taiwan's "drone diplomacy" initiative, Hsiao said the policy presents Taiwan with new opportunities as Beijing has relentlessly tried to sideline Taiwan in the international community. During her visit to Palau in June, Hsiao and Palauan President Surangel S. Whipps Jr. officiated a ceremony at which Taiwan donated four drones to its Pacific ally for patrol and rescue purposes. Hsiao told Radio Taiwan International (RTI) on Aug. 21 that although the drones Taiwan gifted Palau were trainer models, Palau could require drones for other purposes -- for example, when conducting reconnaissance or maritime law enforcement missions, or delivering medicine to remote areas. "I think these capabilities will develop alongside the establishment of Taiwan's domestic manufacturing capabilities and, in the future, could help our diplomatic allies and other countries in the Indo-Pacific that need them."
